subject: Public health
summary: Infection control combines early recognition, appropriate sampling, empiric antimicrobial therapy and source control, adapted to limited diagnostics. In low‑resource settings, clinicians must prioritize bedside clues and simple measures to prevent sepsis and transmission.

sections.p: Infection control is the set of actions to identify, isolate, and treat infectious sources to stop spread and prevent sepsis. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, basic labs and, when possible, cultures.
b: Fever + new local signs (redness, swelling, discharge)
Leukocytosis > 12 × 10⁹/L or left shift
Positive bedside Gram stain or rapid test

sections.p: Severity is staged by the presence of systemic compromise (sepsis, septic shock) and tissue involvement (necrosis, gangrene).
b: Mild‑moderate: localized infection, stable vitals
Severe: systemic inflammatory response, hypotension, organ dysfunction
Critical: septic shock, altered mental status, lactate > 2 mmol/L

sections.p: Common pathogens reflect local epidemiology and wound type.
b: Gram‑positive skin flora (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes)
Gram‑negative enterics (E. coli, Klebsiella) especially in abdominal or urinary sources
Anaerobes (Bacteroides) in deep tissue or necrotising infections
TB, HIV‑related opportunists, malaria‑related secondary bacterial infection in endemic areas

sections.p: Patients may present with a painful, erythematous wound, foul discharge, or systemic signs such as fever, tachycardia, and hypotension.
b: Localized warmth, swelling, and purulent drainage
Rapid progression to skin discoloration, bullae, or gas (necrotising fasciitis)
Systemic: chills, confusion, oliguria

t.b: Identify bloodstream pathogen before antibiotics; guides definitive therapy
Confirms causative organism and resistance pattern
Detect leukocytosis or left shift indicating infection
Screen for tissue hypoperfusion; >2 mmol/L suggests septic shock
Rule out malaria as a co‑trigger of sepsis

sections.p: Failure to control infection can lead to septic shock, multi‑organ failure, and death.
b: Hypotension < 90 mmHg systolic despite fluids
Altered mental status or seizures
Rapidly spreading necrosis or gas in soft tissue
Uncontrolled diabetes or HIV with CD4 < 200 cells/µL

sections.p: Treat the source, start appropriate antibiotics, and support organ function.
b: Empiric IV broad‑spectrum antibiotics covering Gram‑pos, Gram‑neg and anaerobes (e.g., piperacillin‑tazobactam + metronidazole or carbapenem + vancomycin) when necrosis or systemic signs present
Oral amoxicillin‑clavulanate, cephalexin, clindamycin or ciprofloxacin + metronidazole for mild‑moderate infections when IV not needed
Surgical drainage, debridement, or amputation for deep abscess, necrotising fasciitis, wet gangrene
Analgesia with paracetamol ± opioid; avoid NSAIDs until infection source is controlled
Fluid resuscitation 30 mL/kg crystalloid for septic shock, then vasopressors if MAP < 65 mmHg

sections.p: Monitor clinical response, adjust antibiotics when cultures return, and implement basic infection‑prevention measures.
b: Re‑evaluate vitals and wound daily; switch to oral agents after 48‑72 h if improving
Educate patients on wound hygiene, hand washing, and safe dressing changes
Ensure proper sterilisation of instruments; use gloves and masks for all open wounds
Vaccinate staff against hepatitis B and tetanus

sections.p: Distinguish infection control from general wound care and from non‑infectious inflammatory conditions.
b: Cellulitis vs. allergic dermatitis – presence of systemic signs favors infection
Necrotising fasciitis vs. severe cellulitis – pain out of proportion, gas on exam
Septic arthritis vs. gout – joint aspiration shows purulent fluid vs. crystals

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal in early sepsis or in immunocompromised patients.
b: Leukocytosis may be absent in neutropenic HIV patients; rely on vitals and lactate
Blood cultures negative after prior antibiotics; still treat if clinical picture fits
Rapid malaria test can miss low‑parasite loads; consider microscopy if suspicion high

whenToSeekHelp: Progressive tissue necrosis or gas formation

faq.q: When should I start IV antibiotics instead of oral?
faq.a: Start IV when there is tissue necrosis, systemic signs of sepsis, or inability to absorb oral meds.

faq.q: Is it safe to give NSAIDs for pain in an infected wound?
faq.a: Avoid NSAIDs until infection is controlled because they can mask fever and impair platelet function.

faq.q: What if I cannot obtain a culture?
faq.a: Take a deep tissue sample for later transport, start empiric broad‑spectrum therapy, and adjust when results become available.

exam: What is the first bedside step in a patient with a foul‑smelling, rapidly expanding leg wound? — Assess airway, breathing, circulation; obtain vitals, look for systemic signs, and draw blood cultures before antibiotics.
How would you differentiate necrotising fasciitis from severe cellulitis? — Pain out of proportion, tense edema, bullae, crepitus, and rapid progression point to necrotising fasciitis.

A patient with HIV presents with a foot ulcer and fever. Which empiric regimen is most appropriate? — IV piperacillin‑tazobactam + metronidazole (covers Gram‑pos, Gram‑neg, anaerobes) plus surgical debridement if necrosis is present.
Why are NSAIDs avoided in early infection control? — They can mask fever, impair renal perfusion, and increase bleeding risk during surgical debridement.
What laboratory result would prompt you to start vasopressors even after fluid resuscitation? — Persistent MAP < 65 mmHg with lactate > 2 mmol/L despite 30 mL/kg fluids.

If blood cultures are negative but the patient remains septic, what is your next step? — Continue broad‑spectrum antibiotics, reassess source, obtain wound/tissue cultures, and consider imaging for hidden abscess.
Explain why a 6‑week course of antibiotics is required for osteomyelitis. — Bone has poor vascularity; prolonged therapy ensures eradication of organisms embedded in necrotic bone.
What infection‑prevention measures reduce transmission of hepatitis B in the ward? — Use of gloves, safe sharps disposal, hepatitis B vaccination of staff, and proper sterilisation of equipment.
